text: Vertical shallow gully with chockstone. Scramble up good rock and follow the gully system. At steep gully top, exit left into major gully to locate the cannonhole. Crab through the hole beneath an embedded chockstone, then scramble 40 feet of Class 3.5-4.0 rock to summit. Existing rappel slings at multiple points.
runs: scramble up good rock and follow the gully system

text: Mount Saul is the fourth-highest point on Wenatchee Ridge, a spur of the Cascade crest in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It has a bare granitic summit with jagged rocks, a sheer northwest face, and a south side that drops nearly 4,000 ft to Indian Creek Valley in about a mile — the mountain punches well above its modest elevation for alpine character. There is no maintained trail to the top; climbers approach via the Indian Creek Trail from the White River drainage, then leave the trail near Airplane Creek for an off-trail scramble past Airplane Lake to the upper east slopes and summit rocks.
runs: mount saul is the fourth highest point on wenatchee ridge a

text: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. The road is the fragile part, and it is closed right now. Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead. It is not named in the Wenatchee River District storm-damage road order (06-17-07-2026-11, 20 May 2026 through 31 December 2027), which closes seventeen other roads. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.
runs: turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead

text: Most parties base-camp at Seattle Meadows (~4,550 ft), reached via a multi-day approach up the North Fork Quinault River to Low Divide and then west into Seattle Creek Basin. From camp, climb scree slopes on the mountain's western side, cross over a ridge, and continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, finishing with a class 2-3 scramble on the east ridge/side to the craggy summit. Two other approach variants exist (via Noyes Basin, and a more direct line up Seattle Creek Basin itself), converging on the same upper-mountain scramble.
runs: with a class 2 3 scramble on the east

text: From US 101 at the west end of Lake Quinault, near Amanda Park, turn east onto North Shore Road and follow it about 17 miles to its end at the North Fork Quinault trailhead and ranger station. A national park entrance pass is required, plus a wilderness permit for overnight stays.
runs: to its end at the north fork quinault trailhead

text: From US-101 at milepost 126, turn right onto South Shore Road and follow it about 12.9 miles to the Quinault River bridge; cross it, turn right onto North Shore Road, and drive 3.5 miles to the road end at the trailhead.
runs: turn right onto north shore road and drive

text: Drive to Ruth Creek Road's end at Hannegan Campground via Mt. Baker Hwy (SR 542) and Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32)/Ruth Creek Road. From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop southwest to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.
runs: to the base of the couloir at about

text:
Same road access as the Southeast Ridge route: SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) and Ruth Creek Road toward Hannegan Campground. This variant then goes further up the valley before leaving the trail.

From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop southwest to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

One documented attempt turned around near 4,300 ft on rock the party judged unmanageable — mossy, muddy and soaked. That is a real and repeatable outcome rather than an anomaly, and it is the main reason to want this line under snow.
runs: to the base of the couloir at about

text: The standard/easiest and most commonly climbed route on Sefrit. From Ruth Creek, climbers cross the creek and bushwhack up through slide alder to the base of the 'Wall Street' couloir, a roughly 1,500-vertical-foot snow gully about 50 feet wide at 30-35 degrees. The couloir tops out on the Northwest Glacier at about 5,000 ft, crossed (roped, with pickets/flukes for crevasse hazard) to a broad saddle at 6,500 ft just west of the summit. From the saddle, parties either climb a steep, narrow chute due south to a notch just west of the summit pinnacle, or traverse southeast across a shallow snow bowl beneath the summit — the traverse exposes climbers to cornices and is usually roped with snow protection. The route finishes on the southeast ridge: a straightforward Class 2 scramble broken by about 100 ft of exposed Class 3 traversing near the middle. routeFt here (3,691 ft) is a computed total combining the couloir, glacier crossing, and final ridge scramble, since no aggregate route length is known.
runs: to a notch just west of the summit pinnacle or
of exposed class 3 traversing near the middle

text: Southeast ridge scramble from the 6,500-ft saddle to the 7,191-ft summit, including ~100 ft of exposed Class 3 traversing near the middle
runs: of exposed class 3 traversing near the middle

text:
Drive SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to the pullout near milepost 3, just past where a creek flows over a concrete weir, at about 2,950 ft. This is NOT the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of the road.

Cross Ruth Creek. There is no bridge; parties cross on whatever logs are in place, and a three-log cluster has been used. Then about 45 minutes of thrashing through slide alder and devil's club to the avalanche debris at the foot of the snow gully.

The couloir runs roughly 1,500 vertical feet and opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft; from there the route crosses the glacier to a saddle near 6,500 ft and scrambles the southeast ridge to the summit.

Timing is the whole trade: earlier means more snow and more avalanche risk, later means thicker brush and discontinuous snow.
runs: just past where a creek flows over a concrete weir
45 minutes of thrashing through slide alder and

text:
Wall Street is a corridor with walls on both sides, and that is the test. Once you are in it, the gully holds a remarkably uniform gradient of 30-35 degrees and a uniform width of about 50 feet, with very steep rock walls on both sides, for roughly 1,500 vertical feet. Nothing else on this side of the valley does that. In cloud you do not need to see the top: if you can touch rock on your left and rock on your right and the angle is not changing, you are in Wall Street. If your gully fans out, or has a wall on only one side, it is not.

Getting to it: the marker at the bottom is avalanche debris. After the creek crossing and roughly 45 minutes of alder and devil's club, the brush ends at the debris pile at the foot of the snow gully. Debris is what tells you the gully above you actually runs — and it is also the reason to be there early and cold.

The arrival at the top of the couloir is the glacier. The corridor opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft. Walls end, glacier starts.

The discriminator against the peak's other two routes, and it is decided in the car park rather than on the mountain. Three routes on Sefrit start from three different places: this one from the Ruth Creek pullout near milepost 3 on Ruth Creek Road; the Bloody Head Couloir from the Ruth Creek trail higher up the valley near 3,450 ft; and the Southwest Ridge from the Nooksack Cirque trailhead at the end of FR-34, a different road entirely. If you drove to the end of FR-34 you cannot reach this route today.
runs: about 50 feet with very steep rock walls on both sides

text: A steep, seldom-climbed 7,191-foot summit rising abruptly above the North Fork Nooksack River, about three miles north of Mount Shuksan in the Mount Baker Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Whatcom County). Sefrit is notorious among North Cascades climbers less for technical difficulty than for its approach: a brushy, pathless bushwhack up steep timber and slide alder to reach a short but genuine Class 4 ridge/gully system leading to the summit. First climbed in 1930 by Jim Irving and Brick Spouse.
runs: three miles north of mount shuksan in the

text: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 12.5 miles, then turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32). Continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34) and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead, which is a different trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32. Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there's no bridge, so wade it or cross a downed log if one is present, and note that early-summer high water can make the crossing difficult or unsafe.
runs: mile to the junction with nooksack cirque road

text: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR 34), and follow FR 34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (do not confuse with the separate Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR 32). Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge, and early-summer high water can make it difficult or unsafe to cross. Follow the old roadbed/Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west/southwest ridge, passing through/around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system. Above the cliff band, the summit gully splits into several forks; the leftmost fork (or the one just west of a snow couloir to its right) is easiest, and rock is generally solid low but looser near the summit ridge. Note a separate, lower-angle north-side line — via Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier to the SE ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed ~100 ft Class 3 traverse, and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak; don't confuse the two lines when planning.
runs: mile to the junction with nooksack cirque road

text: Rarely climbed; heavy snowfall, avalanche danger, and a highly corniced summit ridge make it a serious, treacherous winter objective.
runs: avalanche danger and a highly corniced summit ridge

text:
From Glacier, drive SR-542 east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34), and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead. This is a different trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32, and from the milepost-3 pullout the Wall Street route uses.

Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge.

Follow the old roadbed and Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west and southwest ridge, passing through or around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system.

A separate, lower-angle line on the north side — Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier, finishing on the southeast ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed Class 3 traverse and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak. The two are easily confused in planning and impossible to confuse on the ground, because they start on different roads.
runs: mile to the junction with nooksack cirque road

text: The route weaves through a steep and exposed chimney system on the Shuksan Arm, briefly touching the top of White Salmon Glacier, up a steep snow slope (Winnie's Slide), across the Upper Curtis Glacier, and up Hell's Highway to Sulphide Glacier before finishing at the 3/4 class summit pyramid. Most parties take 2-3 days.
runs: weaves through a steep and exposed chimney system on the shuksan arm briefly
the top of white salmon glacier up a steep snow slope

text: Ascend roughly 1,000 ft of class 3-4 scrambling through the chimneys (watch for rockfall from parties above), then continue up snow to a high camp at the top of the chimneys below Winnie's Slide (~6,700 ft).
runs: 1 000 ft of class 3 4 scrambling

text: Ascend roughly 1,000 ft of class 3-4 scrambling through the chimneys (watch for rockfall from parties above), then continue up snow to a high camp at the top of the chimneys near the White Salmon Glacier, below Winnie's Slide (~6,700 ft).
runs: 1 000 ft of class 3 4 scrambling

text: Finish on the east ridge of the summit pyramid: roped rock climbing at about 5.3 to 5.6 to the summit. Descend the pyramid's central gully on its south side.
runs: on the east ridge of the summit pyramid

text:
Price Lake must stay below you and to your north-east, and that is the test. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

Arrival: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the shoulder — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

The error that kills people here is drifting left, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay right during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

After 500 ft of traverse the line goes up, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.
runs: the white salmon cirque from the price glacier cirque

text: Follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile, then drop off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climb to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area. Follow that crest to the base of the mountain's north side and gain the northwest arete, a long line of loose, runout rock, moderate ice and glacier travel, to the summit.
runs: to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area follow

text: Two realistic approach options both start by parking at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR 542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and following a dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. The more direct option drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area, then follows the ridgecrest to the base of the mountain's north side. The alternative continues up the road as far as it goes, then travels off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier. From there, gain the crest of the northwest arête itself -- a long, remote line combining bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel.
runs: by parking at the lower white salmon lodge
and following a dirt road up the white salmon
to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area

text: Descend the summit pyramid by its central gully on the south side, then follow the Fisher Chimneys descent: down Hell's Highway onto the Upper Curtis Glacier and across to the top of Winnie's Slide. Descend Winnie's Slide (steep snow, occasionally icy enough to rappel) to the head of the White Salmon Glacier, then go down the glacier as directly as the crevasses allow to the lower White Salmon Glacier and out the White Salmon Creek valley to the road. Expect open crevasses and weak snow bridges on the White Salmon late in the season, and brush in the lower valley once the snow is gone.
runs: follow the fisher chimneys descent down hell's highway
crevasses allow to the lower white salmon glacier

text:
Park at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. This first stretch is common to both options.

The direct option then drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area, then follows that crest to the base of the mountain's north side.

This is a long Cascade adventure route rather than a line with a bootpack: bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel, all in one day.
runs: to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area

text: Above the schrund, climb the steep snow or ice field to the glacier plateau below the summit pyramid, then cross the plateau and swing around to the pyramid's south side. Crevasses remain on the plateau, and the snow here softens early on a warm day.
runs: the steep snow or ice field to the

text: The Sulphide Glacier is the most straightforward glacier route on Mount Shuksan and the standard line for many parties, especially as a ski mountaineering objective in spring. It climbs the broad southern glacier to the base of the summit pyramid, finishing with the same rock scramble shared by other routes.
runs: glacier to the base of the summit pyramid

text: From the campsites (about 6,200 ft for the lower camp), head north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier up rolling steps. At approximately 7,600 feet, terrain flattens and route continues northeast toward summit pyramid. The finish climbs the 3rd-4th class central gully up the south face of the summit pyramid.
runs: head north up the west side of the sulphide glacier up rolling steps

text: Rope up at camp and climb north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier over a series of rolling steps; near 7,600 ft the angle eases, so bear north-northeast across the upper glacier to the foot of the summit pyramid at about 8,400-8,500 ft. Cross the moat and climb the central gully on the pyramid's south face, the one with rappel anchors, roughly 600 ft of steep snow or blocky rock to the summit.
runs: north up the west side of the sulphide glacier

text: Rope up at camp and climb north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier over a series of rolling steps. Near 7,600 ft the angle eases; bear north-northeast across the flatter upper glacier to the foot of the summit pyramid around 8,400-8,500 ft. Large crevasses lie near high camp, bridges thin and blue ice appears as summer goes on, and old GPS tracks stop matching the open cracks late in the season.
runs: north up the west side of the sulphide glacier

text: Climb Hell's Highway, a short chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, watching for a moat where snow meets rock, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid and finish by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class) or the West Ridge (4th class).
runs: the upper west edge of the sulphide glacier

text: Climb Hell's Highway, a short (about 60 m) chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Watch for a moat where snow meets rock. Then follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid.
runs: the upper west edge of the sulphide glacier

text:
Stand at Lake of the Angels and the cirque itself tells you which way to go: Mount Stone is on your right, another peak is on your left, and Mount Skokomish is straight ahead. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

The turn is around the right-hand side of the lake, on a way trail heading west to the ridge. Then take a broad gully southwest and up toward the saddle just north of point 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud.

Second test, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours south and southwest across scree, grass and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn. The tarn is the confirmation. Turn right and start climbing when you are above the large tarn — that is the trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

Third test, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around left to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has three summit horns and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

A directional warning: contouring too far right (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut west over the ridge instead.
runs: ridge then take a broad gully southwest and
up and around left to the true summit which is large and broad

text:
From the Silver Lake camp the route does not go near a col. Walk round the north side of the lake to its far, south-west end, then head south across moraine and snow, skirting a small rock buttress, to the toe of the glacier at about 7,400 ft. Allow an hour to an hour and a half from camp.

You should be able to see at least the lower glacier from camp, so pick your line onto it before you leave. The ice comes down toward the lake from the north side of the peak; you rope up at its toe and climb it, with no saddle or gully on the way.

The wide gully and the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west belong to the other approach, from the lake on the Depot Creek side. If you are climbing a gully toward a gap, you have left this line.

And the negative marker that matters most: the south-west route on this peak starts at the toe of a different glacier on the other flank, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.
runs: you should be able to see at least the lower

text:
From the Depot Creek camp, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the col.

The fixed point is the same: the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully you came up is the way back to camp; the glacier lies on the far side.

The test that you are at the right gap is that both summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

Do not confuse this start with the south-west route, which leaves the same camp. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. If you have not gained a col, you are not on this route.
runs: north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the

text: From the washout walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur road on the left, follow that spur roughly four minutes to a T-junction, then bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about 35 minutes. That brings you to Monument 65 at the US/Canada border, roughly 45 minutes from the washout, where there is a trail register at the obelisk.
runs: an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for

text: From the col drop about 40 ft and traverse rightward across open slopes to an obvious snow and rock gully, then follow the south ridge on its right side through short Class 2-3 gullies, chimneys and rock ribs. Snow slopes steepen to 35 to 40 degrees near the top. For the final hundred feet cross left, with a brief traverse above a remnant snow patch and an easy scramble up a steep scree chute to the true summit.
runs: an easy scramble up a steep scree chute

text:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
runs: an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for

text: Descent is the same Monitor Ridge line back to timberline and then the Ptarmigan Trail back to Climbers Bivouac — there is no rappelling on this route (0 rappels; it is entirely a walk-off/scramble descent). The critical descent hazard is at the top: the crater rim is corniced with wind-built overhanging snow/ice that has repeatedly broken away, including a fatal collapse and multiple large rim failures in recent years, so the Forest Service and USGS explicitly warn to stay back at least 30 ft (9 m) from the visible rim edge and never approach or stand on a cornice for the crater view. From the true summit, descend back to the false summit and pick up the wood-post line down through the loose pumice/ash upper slopes; below about 7,000 ft the marked posts guide you back toward timberline, but climbers should double-check they're following the correct post line on the way down, since it's easy to wander onto a neighboring, unmarked drainage in poor visibility. Depending on season and snow coverage, glissading is possible on sections of the upper mountain and can significantly speed the descent, but chutes are frequently thin, rocky, and mixed with bare ash/pumice patches later in the season, so glissading should be assessed conservatively (an ice axe for self-arrest is standard kit). Below timberline, follow Ptarmigan Trail #216A back down through the forest to the Climbers Bivouac parking lot.
runs: stay back at least 30 ft 9 m from the visible

text: November 1-March 31: climbing permits are free and self-issued at the Marble Mountain Sno-Park kiosk. April 1-October 31: permits are limited and must be purchased in advance on Recreation.gov (released one month at a time), since the quota season applies mountain-wide regardless of which trailhead is used.
runs: november 1 march 31 climbing permits are free and

text: Camping itself is free, but the parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass, or a small day fee. Separately and unavoidably, a climbing permit is required year round for anyone going above 4,800 feet on the mountain, and camping above 4,800 feet is prohibited outright. From April 1 to October 31 that permit carries a daily quota and a per-climber fee of about twenty dollars: 350 climbers a day from April 1 to May 14, then only 110 a day from May 15 through October 31. Permits are sold first come, first served with no lottery, released a month at a time on the first day of the preceding month at seven in the morning Pacific time, and the summer dates sell out within minutes of release. From November 1 to March 31 the permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead with no quota. Blue bags are mandatory for all human waste above the tree line and are stocked at the trailhead kiosk.
runs: on the first day of the preceding month

text: Start at Marble Mountain Sno-Park (about 2,700 ft). Follow Swift Ski Trail #244 north through dense forest to timberline. Cross to the west side of Swift Creek above Chocolate Falls (3,700 ft). Navigate rocky lava flows and mudflows marked by wooden cairn posts up to approximately 4,800 feet. Continue ascending marked route to a seismic station at 6,200 feet. Final snowfield ascent leads to crater rim at 8,363 feet.
runs: swift ski trail 244 north through dense forest to
timberline cross to the west side of swift creek

text: Follow the Swift Creek Trail #244 north through forest about 2 miles to treeline near Chocolate Falls (about 3,700 ft) and cross to the west side of Swift Creek just above the falls. Follow posts, then cairns and wands, up the Worm Flows onto Worm Flow Ridge past the old seismic station near 6,200 ft, join the Monitor Ridge route near 7,400 ft, climb about 850 ft more to the crater rim and walk a quarter mile west along it to the high point.
runs: cross to the west side of swift creek just above

text: From the Marble Mountain Sno-Park (about 2,700 ft) trailhead, the route follows the Swift Creek Trail #244 (blue diamond blazes on trees in winter) north into forest. The trail climbs steadily through timber for roughly 2 miles, gaining to about 3,700-3,750 ft, where it breaks out of the trees near Chocolate Falls, a 40-ft seasonal waterfall on Swift Creek. Just above the falls, cross to the west side of Swift Creek — this ford can be tricky and swollen with meltwater in spring or after warm spells, and the crossing point/sign is often buried in winter snowpack, so treat it as a navigation checkpoint rather than a marked trail junction. Above treeline the route enters the open, barren Worm Flows lava/mudflow terrain; wooden route-marking posts guide climbers from about 3,700 ft up to roughly 4,800 ft, after which large posts thin out and occasional cairns (and, in winter, wands placed by parties) mark the line up broad ridges and open slopes. The route follows Worm Flow Ridge past an old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft, then continues up snow/scree slopes to merge with the summer Monitor Ridge climbing route at about 7,400 ft. From that junction it's another ~850 ft of climbing on open slopes to the crater rim, then about a quarter mile west along the rim to the true summit (8,363 ft). There is no reliable water past Swift Creek/Chocolate Falls, so carry everything you'll need for the round trip. Above treeline this is committing, exposed terrain: whiteout conditions, wind, and snow-covered cairns/posts make route-finding the main crux, so carry a map/GPS track as backup even though the line is well-established. Open slopes on the upper mountain can be avalanche terrain when wind-loaded — avoid loaded slopes and gully bottoms after new snow or wind events.
runs: cross to the west side of swift creek
west along the rim to the true summit

text: From Cougar, drive east on Lewis River Road, which becomes Forest Road 90, to the junction with Forest Road 83; turn left and go about 6 miles to the Marble Mountain Sno-Park. Forest Road 83 is gated at the sno-park in winter and early spring.
runs: cougar drive east on lewis river road which
forest road 83 is gated at the sno park

text:
From the Marble Mountain Sno-Park at about 2,700-2,800 ft, follow the Swift Creek Trail #244 north into forest, marked in winter by blue diamond blazes on the trees. It climbs steadily through timber for roughly 2 miles to about 3,700-3,750 ft, breaking out of the trees near Chocolate Falls on Swift Creek.

Just above the falls, cross to the west side of Swift Creek. This ford can be swollen with meltwater in spring or after a warm spell, and the crossing point and its sign are often buried in winter snowpack.

Above treeline the route enters the open barren Worm Flows lava and mudflow terrain. Wooden posts mark the line from about 3,700 to roughly 4,800 ft; above that the posts thin out and occasional cairns, plus wands placed by parties, mark broad ridges and open slopes. The route follows Worm Flow Ridge past an old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft, then up snow and scree to merge with the summer Monitor Ridge line at about 7,400 ft, and roughly 850 ft more to the crater rim.

A Sno-Park permit is required to park in the winter months. This is the standard winter and spring access because the summer trailhead on the far side is snow-gated.
runs: cross to the west side of swift creek

text:
Three hard markers, in order, and they work because they are objects rather than descriptions of slope — which matters here, since snow buries everything else.

One: Chocolate Falls, at about 3,700-3,750 ft, where the trail breaks out of the trees. You cross to the west side of Swift Creek just above the falls. In winter the crossing point and its sign are usually under snow, so treat the falls themselves as the marker and never a sign.

Two: wooden posts, from about 3,700 to about 4,800 ft. Above 4,800 they thin to cairns and wands.

Three: the old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft on Worm Flow Ridge. This is the last hard object on the whole route and the best single confirmation you are on the ridge and not on one of the broad open slopes beside it.

The negative that catches parties low: if you have crossed Swift Creek and are still in trees, you crossed too low — below the falls. Regain the east bank and keep climbing to the treeline break.

The merge at about 7,400 ft is the last check: from there you are on the summer Monitor Ridge line and it is roughly 850 ft to the rim.

The most important finding on this route is about coming down, not going up. Whiteout wrong-drainage descents are the documented failure here. From the rim the correct line is back down Worm Flow Ridge — a ridge, not a gully. Do not descend into a gully because it is going downhill; and record your bearings on the way up while you can still see the ridge you are on.
runs: cross to the west side of swift creek just above

text: From Marmot Lake Camp (~4,400 ft) leave the maintained trail and follow a small creek up into an amphitheater on the west side of the peak; easy Class 1 slopes lead from the amphitheater to the summit. The multi-day approach up the Duckabush valley (roughly 21-23 trail miles one-way to Marmot Lake) is the real crux of the trip, not the summit scramble itself. An alternate approach from the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish side reaches First Divide, drops into a basin with an unnamed lake, and climbs the saddle between Mount Duckabush and Mount Steel before turning north along the ridge to the summit block; the park lists that trail closed between the Staircase Rapids Loop and Home Sweet Home since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, which leaves the Duckabush/Marmot Lake line as the open approach.
runs: north along the ridge to the summit block the

text: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. The approach is the obstacle, not the climbing. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire: the park still lists the North Fork Skokomish and Home Sweet Home trails closed, with no reopening date, on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and while they stay closed this is the direct way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.

text: The drive ends at the gate where Olney Creek Road leaves the Sultan Basin Road, and the day starts on foot up the closed roadbed. Walk the road uphill for about 4.8 miles, past a first switchback and on to a second one where the grade noticeably eases around 3,700 ft — that second switchback is the key junction and there is nothing signed about it. Mapped road alignments in this area are known to be wrong, so trust the switchback you can see on the ground over the line drawn on a map. Leave the road there and pick up an unsigned but well-established boot path on the right, north side, which climbs onto a forest ridge crest and follows it. The path fades out somewhere around 4,050 to 4,200 ft; from there leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake. Pass the lake on its east side, follow the drainage above it to a cluster of small tarns, and then work up and around toward the bowl directly beneath the summit block. This mid-mountain sequence — road to ridge path to cross-country bench — is the crux of the walk-in and is easy to lose in fog or on a first visit.

text: Follow the Putvin Trail #813 up the west side of Boulder Creek, then switchback steeply to the old Boulder Creek road; turn left and walk downhill about 200 yards to where the trail resumes. Keep climbing steeply to a meadow, scramble the root-and-rock headwall, and continue past the Pond of the False Prophet, which is not the lake, to Lake of the Angels in its cirque below Mount Stone.

text: Near 8,000 ft cross a minor rib to climber's left and continue up loose sand and scree. Toward the head of the couloir, climb boulders to a shoulder, skirt the lingering snowfield along its edge, and continue to a height of land near 8,500 ft below the false summit. Carry axe and crampons into midsummer for the snow, which is dangerous to fall on when firm.
runs: climber's left and continue up loose sand and scree

text: About 100 ft below the false summit on its left is a good spot to leave packs. Scramble through a notch near 9,000 ft beside the false summit, then make a rising traverse northwest along the exposed summit ridge to the true summit (9,415 ft). In spring this ridge can hold steep snow. On the way down, stay high through that same notch; dropping off too early leads into the wrong couloir.
runs: the false summit then make a rising traverse

text: A steep, clean rock pillar rising out of the Ice Cliff Glacier on Mount Stuart's northeast face, first climbed by Kit Lewis and Jim Nelson in 1983. After climbing the access ramp onto the upper Ice Cliff Glacier from the lower North Ridge, four easy pitches lead to the base of the pillar, followed by three sustained crack-climbing crux pitches, then easier climbing to the main false summit above the glacier — 11 pitches in all.
runs: climbing to the main false summit above the glacier

text: Shuffle left about 10 feet to a thin crack; finger jams lead to a rest right before the crux, protected by a fixed stopper, then thin hands to a hand crack and a better belay.

text: The couloir exits through a cornice onto the south-facing ridge just below the false summit at about 8,600 ft. When the cornice is large this is the hardest part of the climb: loose, near-vertical snow needing careful tool work. Look right for a smaller break before tunnelling or climbing the steepest section.

text:
The north ridge rock rib is the discriminator, not the look of the ice. Standing in the 5,400 ft basin facing the mountain, in order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, then the Stuart Glacier beyond it.

So: if that rib is on your right, you are on the Ice Cliff. If you have walked around the rib and it is now on your left, you are on the Stuart Glacier and have gone too far west. If there is no hanging ice anywhere above you and the slope is a uniform moderate angle, you are on the Sherpa and have gone too far east.

The name is the second test. Ice Cliff is the only one of the three carrying a hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. Sherpa has none.

The move itself: walk the moraine up to the foot of the North Ridge, then cut hard left and traverse east under the ice cliff at about 6,600 ft. You are aiming under the cliff, not up the rib.

Touch test at the base, and it is unmistakable in cloud: the ground is not clean snow. It is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen chunks of glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of snow and ice. Standing on that is direct evidence you are underneath the ice cliff.

Both the far left and the far right side of the icefall are used, and which one goes is a conditions question rather than a route question. The same is true of the bergschrund: one published description passes it on the climber's right, another on the left. Do not treat either as fixed, and look before committing.

Exit: surmounting the cornice puts you on the south-facing ridge just below the false summit near 8,600 ft. Standard descent is the Sherpa Glacier, immediately east of the couloir exit, starting around 8,200 ft and dropping back into the same basin — so a party reversing the Ice Cliff is doing something unusual.
runs: the south facing ridge just below the false summit

The only rappel on the route is optional and on the way up: a ~75 ft rappel off the right side of the ridge below the Great Gendarme, from an established fixed sling (not bolted), used to bypass the 5.9 crux pitches. A single 60m rope doubled covers it.

text: Primary approach is from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached via Icicle Creek Road and FR 7601 out of Leavenworth). From the trailhead, follow the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail as it rolls along Mountaineer Creek through forest; at the signed junction roughly 2 miles in, stay right on the Stuart Lake Trail (the Colchuck Lake Trail is the left fork). Continue up the Mountaineer Creek valley on the Stuart Lake Trail, then leave the maintained trail before reaching Stuart Lake itself, cross Mountaineer Creek, and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. After roughly 2 more miles of streamside travel, climb a steep, loose talus/boulder slope to gain the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier — this valley has good bivy sites and is a common overnight stop. From the valley, angle directly up to the toe of the North Ridge, keeping the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left; the notch/base of the upper ridge sits around 8,200 ft, where a snow-filled gully (often climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) gains the crest. All-in this is roughly 6-6.5 miles and 3,300+ ft of gain, about 4-5 hours to the base of the climbing. A well-known alternative is the southern approach via the Esmeralda/Teanaway trailhead over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, gaining the ridge from that side (~9 miles, ~4,800 ft gain, ~8 hours) — longer and higher-gain on the way in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop for parties planning to descend the Cascadian Couloir, since that descent drops back toward Ingalls Creek. Water is available at Mountaineer Creek and its south fork on the north approach, and at Ingalls Creek/seasonal snow patches near the 8,200 ft notch bivy on the south approach; above the notch there is no reliable water. Route-finding through the boulder/talus slope below Sherpa Glacier and the creek crossing (higher and faster in early season) are the main approach-specific hazards.
runs: ridge keeping the ice cliff glacier on your left

text: Nearly all parties descend via the Cascadian Couloir on the mountain's south side — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (0 rappels) under normal summer conditions. From the true summit, downclimb steep snow or scree, keeping right through sparse trees to drop into the head of the Cascadian Couloir, then follow the couloir down its full length (loose sand, scree, and rockfall-prone rock the entire way; an ice axe, and often crampons, are recommended into mid-summer for a lingering snow tongue) to the valley floor near Ingalls Creek, roughly 4,000 ft below the summit. The upper couloir splits into a confusing maze of climbers' paths and cairns — keep to the established talus path on the climber's left side around the 8,800 ft permanent snowfield; parties who drift onto the right side have run into old rappel-station remnants and much harder downclimbing. Because the North Ridge is climbed from the north (Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek side) while the Cascadian Couloir exits to the south (Ingalls Creek/Teanaway side), most parties face a long, tiring hike back around the mountain to a north-side vehicle — either via Longs Pass and a car shuttle, or a full trail loop back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead; parties using the southern (Esmeralda/Longs Pass) approach avoid this by parking on that side to begin with. Note: some parties opt for a short, optional ~75 ft rappel off the right side of the ridge below the Great Gendarme (using an established, well-traveled sling/fixed anchor, not bolted) to bypass the crux 5.9 pitches during the ascent — this is a mid-route bypass rappel, not part of the standard descent, and is not counted in the rappel total below. A single 60m rope doubled (or a single-strand lower) is sufficient for it.
runs: off the right side of the ridge below the

text:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
runs: the stuart glacier staying above the large moraine mound

text: A classic steep snow-and-ice couloir splitting the north side of Mount Stuart above the Stuart Glacier, first climbed by Helmy Beckey and Larry Strathdee in June 1944. Most of the route climbs at 40-50°, with a narrow, sustained crux about halfway up that frequently holds around 100 ft of water ice up to 60°. The route tops out at or near the small notch on the West Ridge route; the exit rock is low 5th class on the standard finish, about 5.7 on the left-side variation.
